transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I’m Dr. [Your Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, the main reason I came in is… I keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t be forgetting. It’s been getting frustrating, honestly. Like I’ll have a heart follow-up appointment, something important, and it’ll just slip right past me unless somebody reminds me or I’ve got it written somewhere I actually remember to look. Or the clinic will call and I’m supposed to call them back, and I’ll think, “I’ll do that in a minute,” and then next thing I know it’s a day later or longer.

And it’s not just medical stuff. Even with little repair jobs, I’ll show up and realize I brought the wrong tool or forgot the one thing I needed, and then I’ve got to go back or waste time. It makes me feel kind of foolish because these are normal everyday things, you know? I’m not working now, but I still try to keep up with my appointments and odds and ends, and it’s like my mind just doesn’t hold onto it the way it should.
How long have you been experiencing these memory problems, and have you noticed them getting worse over time?

It’s been… I’d say it’s really been causing me trouble for about a year and a couple months now. Maybe fourteen months, give or take. I mean, I can’t say I was ever perfect with remembering every little thing, but it became something I couldn’t just brush off after my cardiac scare.

After that happened, I had to cut back on the walking and little projects I used to do, the things that kind of kept my day structured and kept me settled, if that makes sense. Once that changed, it was like the forgetting started standing out more, and then it started interfering more. So yes, over time it feels like it’s gotten worse, or at least it’s become much more of a real problem in my day-to-day life since then.
Have you been feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy during this time?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way, doctor. I mean, I get frustrated, sure—anybody would when they keep dropping the ball on things they used to handle better. And there are days I feel kind of discouraged about it, like, “Why can’t I just remember a simple thing?” But feeling hopeless… no, I don’t think that’s really it.

As far as losing interest, I haven’t really noticed that in the sense of not caring about things anymore. It’s more that I get annoyed with myself when I mess something up or forget something. But I wouldn’t say I’ve been sitting around feeling down all the time or that everything feels pointless. It’s more aggravation than sadness, if that makes sense.
Have you had days where you feel like nothing gives you pleasure, even things you used to enjoy?

I don’t think so, not in that way. I mean, I have off days like anybody, where I’m irritated or I don’t feel like doing much, but I wouldn’t say things give me no pleasure. If something goes well or I get to do something I like, I can still enjoy it.

It’s more that the frustration gets in the way sometimes. Like if I’m trying to do something and I realize I forgot part of it or I’m not prepared, then the whole thing gets soured because I’m annoyed with myself. But that’s different from feeling like nothing is enjoyable anymore, I think. I haven’t really noticed that kind of empty feeling you’re asking about.
Have you found yourself not caring as much about things you used to care about, or not bothering to do things because they don’t seem worth the effort?

I don’t think that’s really what’s happening with me. I mean, I still care about the things I cared about. If something matters, it still matters to me. I don’t have that feeling of, “What’s the point, why bother,” at least not in a broad way.

Now, I’ll admit there are times I put things off or I don’t get around to something, but it’s not because I decided it wasn’t worth the effort. It’s more like I get irritated or I lose track of what I meant to do, and then later I’m annoyed because I did care about it and still didn’t do it. So if anything, the caring is still there—that’s part of why it bothers me when I don’t follow through.

But no, I haven’t noticed myself becoming indifferent or not caring the way you’re describing. It’s more frustration than not caring.
Have you found yourself not feeling motivated to do things, even things you used to look forward to?

I’m not sure I’d call it a lack of motivation exactly. I still look forward to things, at least once I’m actually thinking about them or once they’re in front of me. It’s more like sometimes I don’t get myself moving the way I mean to, and then it can look like I’m not motivated, but inside I don’t feel like I’ve stopped caring or stopped wanting to do things.

Like, if there’s something I normally enjoy, I don’t think, “Oh, I don’t want that anymore.” It’s more that I might get hung up, or distracted, or I just don’t start when I should, and then I get irritated with myself because I did want to do it. So no, I haven’t really noticed that things I used to look forward to suddenly don’t appeal to me. I wouldn’t describe it that way.
Have you noticed yourself not caring as much about things in general, or feeling indifferent even when things are happening around you?

No, I don’t think so. I wouldn’t say I feel indifferent to things happening around me. I notice what’s going on, and I still react to it. If something good happens, I can feel pleased about it, and if something goes wrong, I definitely care—sometimes probably too much in the moment.

I mean, there are times I might seem like I’m not paying attention or I’m off in my own head, but that’s not because I don’t care. It’s more that my mind is somewhere else for a bit, or I’m thinking about one thing and miss another. But emotionally, I don’t feel numb or like nothing matters.

So, no, I haven’t really noticed a general “I don’t care” feeling. It’s more that I can get scattered or frustrated, but I still care about things.
Have you found yourself getting confused or disoriented in places you know well, like your neighborhood or home?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, I know my home, I know my neighborhood, and I haven’t had that experience of looking around and not knowing where I am or feeling lost in a place I should recognize.

Sometimes I might go into a room and think, “What did I come in here for?” but that’s different from being disoriented, I think. I’m not standing there confused about where I am. And if I’m out somewhere familiar, I haven’t found myself unable to figure out how to get back or anything like that.

So, no, I haven’t noticed anything like getting confused in familiar places.
Have you had any trouble figuring out distances, judging depth, or recognizing familiar objects by sight?

No, I don’t think I’ve had trouble with that. I mean, I can judge steps and curbs and things like that well enough, as far as I can tell. I’m not bumping into furniture because I misjudge where it is, and I don’t think I’m having trouble recognizing objects by looking at them.

Sometimes I might misplace something or overlook it if it’s sitting right in front of me, but that feels more like I’m not focusing on it, not that I can’t recognize what I’m seeing. Like, if I look at a chair or my keys or a cup, I know what it is. And I haven’t noticed walls or doorways or stairs looking strange or flat or anything like that.

So, no, nothing like trouble with depth or recognizing familiar things by sight that I’ve noticed.
Have you had trouble doing things you’ve done many times before, like preparing a meal, following a recipe, or handling your medications, where you used to be able to do it without thinking?

No, I don’t think so—not in the sense of forgetting how to do something I’ve known how to do for years. Like, if I’m making something to eat, I still know what steps go with what, and I don’t feel like I’m suddenly confused by the whole process.

With recipes, I mean, I might have to reread a line if I’m not paying close enough attention, but I don’t feel like I can’t understand what it’s asking me to do. And with things I’m used to handling, I haven’t noticed myself suddenly being unable to manage them in the way you’re describing.

So I wouldn’t say I’ve had trouble doing familiar tasks that I used to do automatically. If anything, sometimes I need to slow myself down or check what I’m doing, but I don’t feel like I’ve lost the ability to do those things.
Have you had trouble planning or organizing things that used to feel straightforward, like managing your schedule, handling bills, or putting together a project that takes several steps?

I’m not really sure I’d say that’s changed in a big way. I mean, planning and organizing have never been my favorite things, if I’m being honest, but I don’t know that I’ve noticed a new problem where things that used to be easy suddenly feel confusing or impossible.

With schedules, bills, or something with a few steps, I can usually work through it if I take my time. Sometimes I might have to write things down or look back over what I’m doing, but I don’t feel like I’ve lost the ability to plan it out. It’s more like I need to keep myself from rushing or getting ahead of myself.

So, no, I wouldn’t say I’ve had a major new trouble with organizing things that used to be straightforward. I can still manage those things, maybe just not always as neatly as someone else might.
Have you had any trouble performing tasks that require coordination, like dressing yourself, using tools, or handling everyday objects, even though your hands and arms feel normal?

No, I don’t think I’ve had trouble like that. I mean, I can get dressed normally, button things, use a fork or a screwdriver or whatever around the house, and I don’t feel like my hands aren’t doing what I want them to do.

Sometimes I might fumble with something if I’m rushing or not paying attention, like dropping my keys or having to try again with a small cap or something, but that doesn’t feel like a coordination problem exactly. My hands and arms feel normal, and I haven’t noticed myself suddenly not knowing how to use everyday objects.

So, no, nothing major there that I’ve noticed.
Has anyone close to you, like a family member or close friend, mentioned that they’ve noticed a change in your memory or thinking abilities?

Not really, no. I mean, nobody close to me has sat me down or said, “I’m worried about your memory,” or anything like that. My family might tease me about little things now and then, the way families do, but I don’t think anyone has pointed out a real change in my thinking or memory.

I guess if they have noticed something, they haven’t made a point of telling me. But from what I know, no, I haven’t had anyone say they’re concerned or that I seem different that way.
Have you noticed yourself having trouble with things like finding the right words when you're speaking, making decisions, or understanding something that used to make sense to you?

I don’t think so, not in any big way. I mean, I have the normal moments where a word is right there and I’m sort of waving my hand like, “You know, that thing,” and then it comes to me a second later, but I don’t feel like I’m suddenly unable to talk or explain myself.

Decisions… I can go back and forth sometimes, especially if there are too many options, but I wouldn’t say that’s new or that I can’t decide things I used to handle. And understanding things, no, I haven’t noticed that something that used to make sense to me now just doesn’t. If I slow down and pay attention, I can usually follow it.

So I’d say no, I haven’t really noticed a clear problem with finding words, making decisions, or understanding things. Nothing that feels like a major change.
Have you had any trouble recognizing familiar faces or places, or telling the difference between colors or patterns that you used to have no problem with?

No, I don’t think I’ve had trouble with that. I recognize people I know, like family or neighbors, and I’m not getting lost in familiar places or anything like that. If I see someone out of context, like running into somebody from one place in a totally different place, it might take me a second to place them, but I think that’s pretty normal.

Colors and patterns, no, I haven’t noticed any change there either. I can tell colors apart, match things well enough, read signs, notice patterns on clothes or furniture, that sort of thing. I mean, my eyes aren’t perfect at my age, but as far as recognizing faces or places, or mixing up colors and patterns in a way that worries me, no, I haven’t noticed anything like that.
Have you had any trouble judging distances, such as when parking, going down stairs, or stepping onto a curb, that you didn’t used to have before?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, parking has never been my favorite thing in the world, especially in a tight spot or if there are cars behind me and I feel rushed, but I wouldn’t say I’m misjudging distances in a new way. I’m not bumping into things or clipping curbs or anything like that.

Stairs and curbs seem okay too. I might take my time a little more than I used to, just because I don’t want to be careless, but I haven’t noticed myself stepping wrong because I can’t judge where the edge is. If it’s dark or the curb is uneven, I’m more cautious, but I think that’s just normal common sense.

So, no, nothing that feels like a change or like my depth perception is off.
Have you noticed any changes in your ability to make sound decisions, solve problems, or think clearly about everyday situations that you used to handle without much difficulty?

I don’t think I’ve noticed a real change there, no. I mean, I can have moments where I overthink something simple, like if I’m comparing two things at the store or trying to figure out the best way to do something around the house, and I’ll sort of go in circles for a bit. But that’s not exactly new for me, and if I slow down, I usually get there.

For sound decisions, I still feel like I know what makes sense and what doesn’t. I’m not suddenly doing things and then thinking, “Why in the world did I decide that?” At least not in a way that feels different from before. And problem-solving, everyday stuff, if something breaks or there’s a bill to sort out or I need to plan an errand, I can handle it. I might talk myself through it more than another person would want to listen to, but I can handle it.

Thinking clearly… I guess if there’s too much going on at once, I can feel a little scattered, but I wouldn’t say I’m confused about normal situations I used to manage. So overall, no, I haven’t noticed a big change in judgment or problem-solving or clear thinking.

Have you noticed yourself forgetting recent conversations or events sooner than you used to, like not remembering something that happened just a day or two ago unless it was written down or someone reminds you?

Yes, that’s actually part of what’s been bothering me enough to come in. It’s not like I forget who people are or where I am, but I’ll forget things I really should be keeping track of. Like I’ve had heart follow-up appointments, and then somehow I don’t have it in my head when I’m supposed to, or I mean to call the clinic back and then the day just goes by and I realize I never did it.

And with practical things too, like if I’m supposed to go do a repair or help with something, I’ll show up and realize I don’t have the right tools with me. Then I’m standing there thinking, “How did I not bring that? That was the whole point.” It’s embarrassing, honestly, because these are not complicated things. They’re normal day-to-day responsibilities, and I feel like I should be better about them.

If it’s written down or someone reminds me, I do better, but if I’m just relying on my head, things slip away faster than I’d like.

Have you noticed any worsening in your ability to remember recent events, such as conversations or tasks from just a few hours ago, even when they’re important or when you’ve tried to remind yourself?

Yes, I have noticed that, and that’s really what brings me in, because it’s not just little “where did I put my keys” stuff. It’s things I really should not be forgetting.

Like with my heart follow-up appointments, I’ll know they’re important, I’ll tell myself, “Okay, don’t forget this,” and then somehow it’s just not in my head when it needs to be. Or I’m supposed to call the clinic back, and I’ll think about it earlier in the day, and then the whole day gets away from me and later I realize, “I never made that call.” And then I feel awful because it’s important, it’s not like I’m forgetting to buy crackers or something.

Same thing with tasks. If I’m going somewhere to fix something or help with a repair, I’ll get there and realize I didn’t bring the right tools. And then I’m standing there feeling stupid, because the tools were the whole reason I went. I may have even reminded myself before leaving, but by the time I’m actually out the door, something slips.

So yes, recent tasks and important things are not sticking the way they should, unless I write it down or someone reminds me. It’s frustrating and honestly kind of embarrassing.

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think so—not in the sense of forgetting how to do something I’ve known how to do for years. Like, if I’m making something to eat, I still know what steps go with what, and I don’t feel like I’m suddenly confused by the whole process.

With recipes, I mean, I might have to reread a line if I’m not paying close enough attention, but I don’t feel like I can’t understand what it’s asking me to do. And with things I’m used to handling, I haven’t noticed myself suddenly being unable to manage them in the way you’re describing.

So I wouldn’t say I’ve had trouble doing familiar tasks that I used to do automatically. If anything, sometimes I need to slow myself down or check what I’m doing, but I don’t feel like I’ve lost the ability to do those things.

doctor.intent: Assess for presence of significant difficulty with planning, organizing, or completing complex tasks, which would help differentiate between F04 (Dementia) and G30.9 (Alzheimer's).
doctor.question: Have you had trouble planning or organizing things that used to feel straightforward, like managing your schedule, handling bills, or putting together a project that takes several steps?

target_item.reason: The question is most directly about planning and organizing multi-step tasks, which is not covered by the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure I’d say that’s changed in a big way. I mean, planning and organizing have never been my favorite things, if I’m being honest, but I don’t know that I’ve noticed a new problem where things that used to be easy suddenly feel confusing or impossible.

With schedules, bills, or something with a few steps, I can usually work through it if I take my time. Sometimes I might have to write things down or look back over what I’m doing, but I don’t feel like I’ve lost the ability to plan it out. It’s more like I need to keep myself from rushing or getting ahead of myself.

So, no, I wouldn’t say I’ve had a major new trouble with organizing things that used to be straightforward. I can still manage those things, maybe just not always as neatly as someone else might.

doctor.intent: Assess for presence of apraxia or difficulty performing purposeful movements despite intact motor function, which is a distinguishing feature of dementia (G30.9) compared to pseudodementia of depression (F04).
doctor.question: Have you had any trouble performing tasks that require coordination, like dressing yourself, using tools, or handling everyday objects, even though your hands and arms feel normal?

target_item.reason: The question asks about coordination or motor/apraxia-like difficulty with dressing, tool use, or handling objects despite normal strength/sensation. The provided ADHD symptom profile does not include a matching coordination or motor planning symptom.

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think I’ve had trouble like that. I mean, I can get dressed normally, button things, use a fork or a screwdriver or whatever around the house, and I don’t feel like my hands aren’t doing what I want them to do.

Sometimes I might fumble with something if I’m rushing or not paying attention, like dropping my keys or having to try again with a small cap or something, but that doesn’t feel like a coordination problem exactly. My hands and arms feel normal, and I haven’t noticed myself suddenly not knowing how to use everyday objects.

So, no, nothing major there that I’ve noticed.

doctor.intent: Ask about the presence of significant memory decline that is corroborated by another person, which would support a diagnosis of major neurocognitive disorder (G30.9).
doctor.question: Has anyone close to you, like a family member or close friend, mentioned that they’ve noticed a change in your memory or thinking abilities?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether others have noticed a change in memory or thinking abilities, which is more about observed cognitive decline than any specific ADHD symptom profile listed.

patient.answer:
Not really, no. I mean, nobody close to me has sat me down or said, “I’m worried about your memory,” or anything like that. My family might tease me about little things now and then, the way families do, but I don’t think anyone has pointed out a real change in my thinking or memory.

I guess if they have noticed something, they haven’t made a point of telling me. But from what I know, no, I haven’t had anyone say they’re concerned or that I seem different that way.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a decline in cognitive abilities beyond memory, such as problems with language, reasoning, or judgment, which would support a diagnosis of dementia (G30.9).
doctor.question: Have you noticed yourself having trouble with things like finding the right words when you're speaking, making decisions, or understanding something that used to make sense to you?

target_item.reason: The question asks about language difficulty, decision-making, or comprehension changes, which are cognitive symptoms not covered by the provided ADHD symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so, not in any big way. I mean, I have the normal moments where a word is right there and I’m sort of waving my hand like, “You know, that thing,” and then it comes to me a second later, but I don’t feel like I’m suddenly unable to talk or explain myself.

Decisions… I can go back and forth sometimes, especially if there are too many options, but I wouldn’t say that’s new or that I can’t decide things I used to handle. And understanding things, no, I haven’t noticed that something that used to make sense to me now just doesn’t. If I slow down and pay attention, I can usually follow it.

So I’d say no, I haven’t really noticed a clear problem with finding words, making decisions, or understanding things. Nothing that feels like a major change.

doctor.intent: Ask about presence of visuospatial deficits, which would support G30.9 (Alzheimer's) over F04 (Organic Amnestic Syndrome).
doctor.question: Have you had any trouble recognizing familiar faces or places, or telling the difference between colors or patterns that you used to have no problem with?

target_item.reason: The question is about visual recognition/perceptual problems such as recognizing faces or places and distinguishing colors or patterns, which are not covered by the ADHD symptom profile provided.

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think I’ve had trouble with that. I recognize people I know, like family or neighbors, and I’m not getting lost in familiar places or anything like that. If I see someone out of context, like running into somebody from one place in a totally different place, it might take me a second to place them, but I think that’s pretty normal.

Colors and patterns, no, I haven’t noticed any change there either. I can tell colors apart, match things well enough, read signs, notice patterns on clothes or furniture, that sort of thing. I mean, my eyes aren’t perfect at my age, but as far as recognizing faces or places, or mixing up colors and patterns in a way that worries me, no, I haven’t noticed anything like that.

doctor.intent: Ask about presence of visuospatial deficits, particularly in judging distances or navigating familiar environments, which can help differentiate between the candidates.
doctor.question: Have you had any trouble judging distances, such as when parking, going down stairs, or stepping onto a curb, that you didn’t used to have before?

target_item.reason: The question is about visuospatial perception or depth/distance judgment, which is not covered by the ADHD symptom profile items provided.

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think so. I mean, parking has never been my favorite thing in the world, especially in a tight spot or if there are cars behind me and I feel rushed, but I wouldn’t say I’m misjudging distances in a new way. I’m not bumping into things or clipping curbs or anything like that.

Stairs and curbs seem okay too. I might take my time a little more than I used to, just because I don’t want to be careless, but I haven’t noticed myself stepping wrong because I can’t judge where the edge is. If it’s dark or the curb is uneven, I’m more cautious, but I think that’s just normal common sense.

So, no, nothing that feels like a change or like my depth perception is off.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a decline in cognitive function beyond memory, such as in reasoning, judgment, or problem-solving, which would support G30.9 (Alzheimer's disease) over F04 (amnestic disorder due to general medical condition).
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your ability to make sound decisions, solve problems, or think clearly about everyday situations that you used to handle without much difficulty?

target_item.reason: The question asks about changes in executive functioning/cognition such as decision-making, problem-solving, and clear thinking, which are not specifically covered by the ADHD symptom profile items provided.

patient.answer:
I don’t think I’ve noticed a real change there, no. I mean, I can have moments where I overthink something simple, like if I’m comparing two things at the store or trying to figure out the best way to do something around the house, and I’ll sort of go in circles for a bit. But that’s not exactly new for me, and if I slow down, I usually get there.

For sound decisions, I still feel like I know what makes sense and what doesn’t. I’m not suddenly doing things and then thinking, “Why in the world did I decide that?” At least not in a way that feels different from before. And problem-solving, everyday stuff, if something breaks or there’s a bill to sort out or I need to plan an errand, I can handle it. I might talk myself through it more than another person would want to listen to, but I can handle it.

Thinking clearly… I guess if there’s too much going on at once, I can feel a little scattered, but I wouldn’t say I’m confused about normal situations I used to manage. So overall, no, I haven’t noticed a big change in judgment or problem-solving or clear thinking.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a decline in memory that affects daily life, particularly in recalling recent events or conversations, which could further support a diagnosis of dementia (G30.9) over a depressive disorder (F04).
doctor.question: Have you noticed yourself forgetting recent conversations or events sooner than you used to, like not remembering something that happened just a day or two ago unless it was written down or someone reminds you?

target_item.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is I keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t, like heart follow-up appointments, calling the clinic back, or showing up with the right tools for a repair job.
target_item.reason: The question is directly about forgetting recent conversations or events and needing reminders, which best matches the profile item on forgetfulness in daily activities.

patient.answer:
Yes, that’s actually part of what’s been bothering me enough to come in. It’s not like I forget who people are or where I am, but I’ll forget things I really should be keeping track of. Like I’ve had heart follow-up appointments, and then somehow I don’t have it in my head when I’m supposed to, or I mean to call the clinic back and then the day just goes by and I realize I never did it.

And with practical things too, like if I’m supposed to go do a repair or help with something, I’ll show up and realize I don’t have the right tools with me. Then I’m standing there thinking, “How did I not bring that? That was the whole point.” It’s embarrassing, honestly, because these are not complicated things. They’re normal day-to-day responsibilities, and I feel like I should be better about them.

If it’s written down or someone reminds me, I do better, but if I’m just relying on my head, things slip away faster than I’d like.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms continue to align with both F04 (Organic amnestic syndrome) and G30.9 (Alzheimer's disease, unspecified) as there is persistent difficulty with memory for recent events and tasks, without clear progression to more global cognitive decline or additional neuropsychiatric features. No new information sufficiently rules out either diagnosis at this time.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences memory impairment severe enough to meet criteria for dementia (G30.9) versus a milder cognitive disorder (F04).
doctor.question: Have you noticed any worsening in your ability to remember recent events, such as conversations or tasks from just a few hours ago, even when they’re important or when you’ve tried to remind yourself?

target_item.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is I keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t, like heart follow-up appointments, calling the clinic back, or showing up with the right tools for a repair job.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about worsening memory for recent tasks and important reminders, which most directly matches forgetfulness in daily activities such as missing appointments, failing to return calls, or forgetting needed items.

patient.answer:
Yes, I have noticed that, and that’s really what brings me in, because it’s not just little “where did I put my keys” stuff. It’s things I really should not be forgetting.

Like with my heart follow-up appointments, I’ll know they’re important, I’ll tell myself, “Okay, don’t forget this,” and then somehow it’s just not in my head when it needs to be. Or I’m supposed to call the clinic back, and I’ll think about it earlier in the day, and then the whole day gets away from me and later I realize, “I never made that call.” And then I feel awful because it’s important, it’s not like I’m forgetting to buy crackers or something.

Same thing with tasks. If I’m going somewhere to fix something or help with a repair, I’ll get there and realize I didn’t bring the right tools. And then I’m standing there feeling stupid, because the tools were the whole reason I went. I may have even reminded myself before leaving, but by the time I’m actually out the door, something slips.

So yes, recent tasks and important things are not sticking the way they should, unless I write it down or someone reminds me. It’s frustrating and honestly kind of embarrassing.

The cognitive decline is not better explained by another mental disorder or neurocognitive condition, and appears to be acquired and not progressive at this time, consistent with amnestic disorder due to general medical condition (F04).
